why.headline: Strong sides keep you long and steady when you land sideways.

claims.text: Dives go sideways, so your sides take the load. In academy keepers, weaker-side dives showed less trunk control.
In elite adult keepers, extra hip and chest turning slowed weaker-side dives.
In the ready stance you hold still, then push off. Coaches of young players train the middle to steady spine and hips.
Pupils in their early teens did trunk exercises twice a week. After 6 weeks, trunk tests were 8 to 22% better.
Early-teen players added five moves, one a side plank, 4 times weekly. After 26 weeks, jumps were 5 to 6.8% higher.

keep_up.text: Keep training it every week to keep gains coming. In one youth study, jump gains lasted 8 weeks after training stopped. Everyone improves at their own pace.

map.plain: The muscles on the sides of your tummy
The muscle on the side of your hip
The long muscle down the front of your tummy

note.text: Side plank studies measured these muscles in adults; none in teens.

claims.text: In adults, the side plank worked side tummy and hip muscles hard. That level suits building strength.
Studies in young people find strength rises far more than muscle size. Early gains are mostly your nerves learning to switch muscles on.

limits.text: No study has tested the side plank alone in goalkeepers. The youth trials used several trunk exercises.
Side planks are part of the FIFA 11+ warm-up. A youth trial linked the whole warm-up to fewer injuries. No trial shows the side plank prevents injury alone.
